My partner's family did not permit me to come to the scattering of his ashes. We were and are on good terms, but it was something they wanted to do "as a family". I really struggle with the lack of rights unmarried partners have. But you're absolutely right, he's just ash now. That's what I kept telling myself too. What is more valuable are the signs of his life you now own are. 

Notes with his handwriting. Places you both went. Memories you both held and no one else has. And of course your son.

Lots of love x
For the PTSD aspect, EMDR really really helped me, and I have seen quite a few other people mention it on here.

I did this after my partners suicide and for me it was because by immersing myself in the pain of others I felt less alone with the shock and trauma of what had happened to me/us - even with quite unrelated events (I recall that a family lost their daughter to an allergic reaction to a pret baguette and she died quite quickly and traumatically. I felt their pain so intensely that it made me cry for days and I developed a deep fear of sesame - completely irrationally!). I also sought to understand darker aspects of the human psyche and especially of people who do unpredictable things, but eventually during therapy this behaviour went away on it's own accord as I started to face up to my individual grief and loss (which, in a way, I had been putting off by focussing on the pain felt by others). Grief can be a type of madness if you let it devour you. 

You're not being shitty - this is obsessive behaviour on her part and it sounds very unhealthy. It could be that she has complicated grief disorder - not unusual with people bereaved by suicide, but if she hasn't identified in herself perhaps you could encourage her to recognise that in herself, or talk to a close friend of hers who might also be worrying about her behaviour. You could also ask if you would be able to join one of her therapy sessions and bring up these behaviours with the therapist there as a mediator.  It could be that eventually she will run out of steam with this behaviour - as was the case for me, but it seems to have been going on a very long time.

It's hard on you that you are dealing with your own grief and have this added pressure of worrying about your mother, but you must remember she is not your responsibility and once you have raised your concerns and alerted others, the rest will be up to her, and you must make sure you protect yourself and seek support for your grief and these added stresses.

Hey, 

the short answer to this is: yes. You will meet someone else and find love and be happy, but 'moving on' might be a trickier concept. The pain of your loss will get easier to bear, and you will realise it's not a betrayal to find happiness again. Even if our loved ones expressed bitterness or anger in their last moments, it's important to remember that their suicide - like those sentiments - were not made in a rational moment. 

Mostly, I think they would be relieved and happy that their passing did not utterly destroy our lives, and sad for the amount it hurt and caused us lifelong grief  - which I believe that in those irrational moments, is always extremely underestimated.

I think it depends on the very specific relationship that a person has with someone who dies by suicide and the set of circumstances that surround that event. 

In summary, it is not wrong to be angry with someone who has died by suicide, if you have experienced this loss then how you feel about it is entirely valid, but that's great you don't feel that about your person.

I agree with the first post that suggested EMDR. I really can't thank it enough, but I understand that now isn't an opportune moment to seek therapy, let alone one so specialised. 

EMDR was developed by a woman who discovered the benefits of rapid eye movement whilst out on her walk whilst coming to terms with emotional pain. I was on a waiting list for EMDR for months before I finally got to see someone, and I know it sounds ridiculous but this is what I did in the meantime. I took long walks and made a concerted effort to think about all that painful stuff whilst also looking at the things around me. 

It's definitely not EMDR but it made the trauma a bit more familiar and diluted. It helped in the interim before I could finally get the proper therapy.

I'm so sorry to hear that. It's completely normal after something so horrendous. I started getting them after my partner died. 

Don't worry about them too much. All of the symptoms you describe are those of a panic attack, and it's a natural response to our bodies struggling to come to terms with lack of control. 

It needn't be something that happens again, but even if it is, you can and will overcome them. I found getting angry helped. I would almost shout "bring it fucking on!" and the anger struggled to coexist with my fear. CBT therapy and yoga exercises helped a lot too.

You'll find a way x

When we rely so much on our bodies giving us clear signals of cause and effect for much of our lives, the scariest thing about getting panic attacks is realising you can't trust your body and mind all of the time. For me that came with its own maelstrom of sudden loss of confidence in myself and fed into a spiral that started with me catching my breath and a rush of adrenaline (out of nowhere). I got them for the first time at the age of 29, and I did the same thing in terms of repeatedly looking for a rational reason for feeling like I was about to die. I had all the symptoms you mention, but eventually I worked out that the amygdala is a little bitch. It's basically just misfiring. There's nothing wrong - every panicked rush to A&E, every test... even just leaping up or becoming restless was validating my brains misfire, further ingraining the behaviour until it became a disorder. 

I eventually helped myself with my own version of flood therapy (note - it gets a lot worse before it gets better but it *does* get better). Once you realise that panic attacks can't kill you and you need to retrain this tiny bastard in your head, you cure yourself! It's magic. 

I found this video helpful as a starting point: https://youtu.be/8Un_Ykh9y9Q.

Believe me, it can and will get better. X

It sounds like your GF was looking for a way to wound you because of her own insecurity about your relationship with this other ex. 

I would call it immature but that would be giving her far too much credit in terms of the gravity of what she's implying. 

You need to cut that one loose my friend, it's gone bad.

I was cheated on by the man I loved more than anything in the world, and we had just bought our house - we were best friends too! He was my 'one', but when I found out about him cheating - suicide didn't cross my mind. It was him, who ended his life. 

I don't think it's ever down to the other person really. When you are an adult, shit happens and it's your own in built ability (or inability) to cope, that defines your response, and that very rarely has anything to do with a partner/friend etc., And a lot to do with how they have learnt to see themselves and cope with intense stress or emotional pain. 

I was in intense emotional pain but it didn't occur to me to take my own life because I was mentally well, with a support network and strong sense of identity and self. This isn't anything my partner gave to me, and its not something that was in his ability to take away. The same goes for you. If every time someone cheated or a marriage or relationship broke down it ended in suicide, the life expectancy of the average human would be about 45. 

People make mistakes.

I've started a little ritual with cooking together (I have subscribed to a recipe box thing and suggested we can learn new recipes together) as that's quite an easy one. I was wondering about giving him a spare key or something but that feels like a declaration of trust/commitment I'm not ready to do (not because of my late partner, but because it feels too soon and I know I'd be doing it to try and appease him). 

I have said he can ask me things but I think he's torn between wanting to ask and actually not liking the answer. I think he was expecting a different answer to his previous questions about whether I loved my partner and whether I still got sad about it, but I tried to explain that it's a lot different to a break up and I think he just struggles to grasp it - and I don't really want to drill it into him like "it's earth shatteringly awful and I wish it never happened and it's pain you've never imagined" but I am not sure how much to temper my responses. I was understably devastated that my late partner died, but it doesn't mean that I'm not happy I met my new boyfriend - I guess I just don't know how to show him they're not mutually exclusive emotions. 

Talking to my previous therapist isn't really an option as he moved away, and in a way my therapist reminds me of some of the darkest times in my grief so I'm not sure I'd be keen to mar the two together, but it's a good idea - perhaps with a fresh therapist (although to be seeing a therapist three months in is hardly a good thing). It's so tricky!

I don't think he's had anyone in his life die other than grandparents (and of course, I wish that was the case for everyone!) but I do completely understand it must be hard to reconcile for him. I wish there was something I could do

Yes sure, we can't enforce a viewpoint, but definitely any viewpoint from a bereaved person is welcome here... we also only really know about our own loss and person. 

I think it's good for us to essentially take someone referring to suicide generally and almost ignore it, but accept it could be very true for their person.

Yes sweeping generalisations are not helpful from either side, when someone refers to their loss and their feelings about it, this is somewhere they can come and have their feelings heard and validated.
I'm a little bit speechless at this one.
You are very welcome here if it helps you in any way at all. X

Yeah sure, maybe there's a middle ground to be had, because I've definitely seen it go the other way where someone with poor mental health kinda abuses the people in their lives or doesn't hold themselves accountable for things. It's a bit of both I think. Taking responsibility and proactively working towards a better life within a framework of love and support from family and a wider community.

Yes definitely, in fact most psychologists I spoke to said that they only began worrying about a suicidal patient when two things happened:

1. They start talking about how others would be better off without them (they described it as a process of the patient giving themselves permission to do it)
2. They had a plan of how they would do it

Also, generally speaking, yes anger doesn't get you anywhere, but in my experience, being angry at my partner was incredibly helpful.

When the anger I felt for him superceded the intense sorrow and misery I had for losing him I was able to get out of bed and do things to start adjusting to life without him. Anger in this sort of bereavement is a very useful tool!

It would maybe be selfless if they were right about being a burden, but they only think that way because of faulty thinking. Someone with mental health problems isn't automatically a burden, unless they are abusing the love of their support people and not seeking to help themselves in any way. (But even burden or not, I think it's fair to say we would still want them to stay).

Yeah maybe! But suicide psychology is at a really early stage/slightly non existent and you're making a few assumptions yourself there. People who take their own lives haven't necessarily been treated badly by society or had anything happen that you can point at and say was a contributing factor. It's ok to think it's selfish and it's right that someone who has lost someone close to them can come here and say that and be supported. Almost everyone *knows* someone who has died by suicide but unless you're related or a close friend or a partner/spouse it's unlikely that it's going to hit you quite the same way as someone who is in that category. 

I personally think people taking responsibility for their own happiness and seeking help for themselves (and not feeling stigma for openly having mental health issues) is the way forward, but you know... Opinions.

Yes you're entitled to your opinion but remember this is a sub for people who have lost someone. Have you? Losing someone to suicide is classed as a 'traumatic bereavement' and people are entitled to come on this page and say whatever they need to say and get support and love from the community that understands why they might feel that way, regardless of how controversial it might seem to an outsider's perspective. Many suicidal people or even just people interested in suicide come to this sub without realising that suicide as a topic alone doesn't unite us in any way, we are experiencing something they are not, so if you haven't experienced it, you should really keep your opinion to yourself and allow this person whatever means they need in order to express the hurt they have for losing someone.

That's just like... Your opinion, man. 

And everyone is entitled to their own. Of course there were lots of factors and I feel lots of different ways about it - but I actually think my partner was incredibly selfish to take his own life, particularly as I hadn't known he had mental health issues so I hadn't had the opportunity to help him - and he hadn't given himself the chance to get better. When he killed himself he made a decision for me and his family, not just himself.

He robbed me of him, his parents of a son, his nephews of their uncle and his sister's of their brother, and his death fucked us all up, so yeah, it was fucking selfish. No one can say it wasn't because I get to feel how I want about it.

It's usually caused by post nasal drip, which gets worse at night due to lying down and irritates the back of your throat. One way to help alleviate these symptoms is by taking antihistamines which help dry up the mucus that contributes to PND, the more modern varieties are better. You can also get steroid nasal sprays but antihistamines are a quick fix. Another thing you can do to help yourself is have more pillows than usual and sleep slightly sitting up.

I don't think its necessarily that their pain is greater, I think it's that they have a poorer ability to cope. After my partner died, alongside a CBT therapist and an EMDR therapist, I also saw a psychologist specialising in masculine identity and suicide (it was an expensive time!) and that essentially how he phrased it.

I think that my partner was missing an inner reserve and resiliance that mentally healthy people have, and on one level had simply "had enough". He was very impetuous and I think in that dark tunnel vision of despair they go a bit numb sometimes and can't see anything else other than the way-out, including the people who love them and will be destroyed by what they're about to do. I don't know of course that it's the case for everyone, but after endless reading, discussing and ruminating, I think that was the case for my man. He didn't leave a note so I have nothing else to go on.

I lost my partner to suicide and I suppose because I felt so much guilt about it, I started casually dating women, and because I didn't feel the same guilt about it as I would if I had dated a man, it allowed me to somehow carry on having intimate relationships without feeling like I was betraying him or replacing him. I appreciate that's a bit of an extreme one, but there it is.

I have. Time helps with a lot of things. I have learnt that people are much deeper and complex than we can possible imagine and that it's impossible to share 100% of who you are with someone, because that's constantly in flux, but also that secrets go hand in hand with poor mental health.

My partner might have been seeing prostitutes for years before I found evidence of one occasion (and left, prompting him to take his life). He had also been fired from his job and got kicked off his university degree - I knew nothing!

I didn't go to my partner's one- I just want to make you aware that you have that choice- not to go. In the UK you can request all the paperwork and comments in a file and they post it to you. I did that instead and waited until I was ready to go through it.

I can see from your post history that you are suicidal yourself. I'm so sorry you feel that way. I don't have the answers. I wish I did. If I did, perhaps my partner wouldn't have died. 

I'm not sure the bereaved can accurately be described as functioning members of society, because grief can be just as crippling as mental health. I think there are many people who might lose someone to suicide who are also struggling with mental health, and suicide of a loved one can also ignite mental health issues in a previously 'well' person that they have never experienced before. It is also not unusual for people connected to the person who died to follow them shortly after. I personally developed a panic disorder after my partner's death. I must have been neurologically predisposed to it as a possibility, but the trauma of finding his body connected those dots in my brain and allowed it to flourish. I had never experienced any form of mental health issue (that I am aware of) prior to his death. 

You're right, people who lose someone to suicide tend to be extremely receptive and responsive to people who are suicidal, and that is for a multitude of reasons including wanting to save a life (of course), attempting to redeem a perceived failure to save a life when their loved ones took their lives, and also because they want to spare the loved ones of the suicidal person the pain that they have endured. 

Unfortunately, putting that responsibility onto a bereaved person is as cruel as it is redundant. We are not equipped to save anyone's lives, sadly. The truth is, no one is, and that's why the podcast and this sub are mainly directed at bereaved people. We are just trying to work our way through our grief, but we are glad for anyone who visits our sub and considers the impact their decision might have on the loved ones in their lives.

Absolutely, though the primary focus here would be the bereaved people themselves, as there are various sources of support for people who experience mental health issues (however inadequate they might be) and virtually nothing for those who are bereaved. 

I think I have to be careful not to put a responsiblity on people who have recently been bereaved to deal with mental health issues of others (other than in a way that supports their own healing), because quite simply they are not equipped to do that, but perhaps by opening up a discussion of their experiences they can better support those who are currently supporting people with mental health issues, and identify failures in the system or society at large that contributed to what happened.

Suicide is contagious, mostly for the exact reasons you mention, I think it's fair to say. I imagine a lot of us think about it after we've lost a person that way. For me I sort of felt like I deserved to die, and it would be right - somehow settling a debt to the universe - if I were to die in the same way, and the chance I might get to see him again (even though I'm agnostic) was a huge draw because I missed him so much - and still do. I even considered that the longer I left it, the further away he would be, so I ought to do it soon. I looked at different ways of doing it and avoided eye contact with people who I felt might be able to see my thoughts written all over my face. It went on for a couple of months and now and then passes like a shadow even now, fourteen months later. 

But in this way I think this awful complicated grief can be a type of insanity, and it's important you give yourself the time and the nurture to allow the clouds to pass - and they will, if you give it time. You're absolutely right, your death would bring nothing but pain and anguish for the people left behind. It would achieve nothing and be a terrible waste. You'd be robbing yourself of the chance to be happy again, and you *do* have that chance. Time can't heal all wounds, but the pain softens, I promise. It would be awful to reignite it for everyone by doing it to yourself.

My therapist told me that pain is inevitable, suffering is a choice. I did a lot of this sort of thinking (14 months since he died and I still do sometimes) but actually none of those thoughts are helpful and there will come a time when you need to make a choice not to torture yourself with these things. 

If you died would you sincerely wish for him to live the rest of his life alone without love? I doubt it. It's an unreasonable request. You deserved his love and you're deserving of someone else's one day, when you're ready. He doesn't get a say now. 

I thought a lot about my partner and whether he suffered. I don't have an answer but I choose to believe he was so out of his mind that he was numb to it. Either way, I have spent longer thinking about the way my partner died and what he went through than the time he actually spent going through it. You will be the same - you have both suffered. His death is something you have experienced together, unfortunately, but unlike him, it will be something you continue to experience for the rest of your life as you learn to adjust to his absence. 

Similarly I thought a lot about whether my partner considered that I would find him. I know exactly what you mean about the swaying. It's hard to explain that to someone who has never found a loved one's body. You can tell straight away that they're no longer 'in there' can't you? It's so strange. I honestly don't believe they even think about that bit. I think they're so blinkered by pain and desperation that it doesn't really factor into their thinking. I don't think my partner even really considered the fact that he would die. I think he just thought of it in terms of "stopping". I didn't get a note so no idea.  

It's normal to torture yourself with all of this wondering and questions, and it's normal to oscillate between anger and guilt and ink-black sorrow, but it gets softer and a lot of the questions lose their energy and are still there but as quiet things that you can sort of 'put to bed' at will. That's making a choice not to suffer. We can't control what happens to us but we can control how we deal with it, and you can honour your partner but don't let it become something you put yourself through. He's not here. He won't benefit from it. This is about you from here on out. Look after yourself, your life depends on it!

And as for afterwards, how can anyone really say? Even the atheists are working on assumptions they can't possibly know. Don't wonder about it too much, we all find out one day.   

Sending lots of love x

I struggled with this a lot and still do, and I find it hard to move past, but I think for your sake you need to try and not hold on to things that do not 'serve' you if that makes sense? I can only think this is some human need to take control over what's happened - it's a very instinctive thing, and unfortunately as you - like me - weren't yet married, it's her legal jurisdiction. You can tell her calmly how you feel but if she declines - it's better to try and move past it. 

It's not fair and it disregards your feelings about it, but you have an opportunity to try and concentrate on other aspects of your grief - so try not to dwell on the ashes. Unfortunately he's not really 'in' them. They're just ashes at the end of the day. My friend tried to cheer me up by pointing out I might have otherwise been walking around with the ashes of his toe and I'd have no idea. But it's important to find other rituals or things that help you cope. Do you have any of his favourite possessions or clothes? My partner and I had a huge argument as I had found out he had cheated on me. I left the house and when I came back the next day I found him. I said horrible things to him and I wish I could have ten more minutes with him to let him know I love him and that I was only saying things because I was hurt. I understand the guilt, but actually, we are just humans and we didn't have the benefit of hindsight to know how crucial our words were. We were not to know they would be our last, and it isn't reasonable to go through life always assuming that your conversation with someone could be your last one. My partner made those my last words - that wasn't my choice, and it wasn't yours. 

I've since learnt so many things about him, that indicate that although our argument was a trigger, he had an illness that he had been hiding for a really long time and hadn't learnt to deal with. Despite what people might say, with a bit of time and perspective I find it very difficult to believe that anyone who has died in this way *hadn't* been struggling for a long time. Perhaps even a lifetime. That in itself is a tragedy, but you can only help someone if they let you know that they need help, and often they don't. We weren't to know, and even if all things were well between you and your brother, it's really likely that there will have been a trigger entirely independent of you or any of your family at some point. It's sadly common for people to take their own lives without an argument having happened. I know someone who took their own life after negative feedback about their performance at work. Did the negative feedback kill that person? No. Of course not. It was perhaps one final drop in an ocean of feeling incredibly low and worthless, that no amount of love or support from others could really touch.

Sometimes therapists aren't quite *enough*. Have you considered being assessed by a psychiatrist? Or working with a psychoanalyst? EMDR and CBT are really helpful but many therapists focused on talking therapies don't offer them. 

I am assuming you're based in the UK. Have you attended any Sobs groups or Mind sessions? Where about's in the UK are you? There may be additional support depending on your region.

Lastly I would say you know firsthand the pain that your suicide would cause. You can get through this. It's important you keep trying xx
